[00:00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, this is a casual chat — we wanna record some of the story behind Vela's move to Redwood, get a couple of soundbites for a case study and the podcast page. If anyone's not comfortable being recorded, shout now.
[00:00:14] Liam: All good, go ahead. Happy to do it.
[00:00:18] Maya: Awesome, quick intro — I'm Maya from Redwood growth, I'll shepherd the case study. Ethan, wanna kick us off with a short prompt?
[00:00:26] Ethan: Yeah, quick high level: can you tell our listeners what Vela does and why inference matters for your product? Liam?
[00:00:34] Liam: Sure. So Vela is a realtime conversational insights platform for customer support teams. We ingest chat and voice, run models to surface intents, summaries, suggested replies. Inference is literally the product — if we're slow or wrong the UX collapses.
[00:00:52] Priya S.: We care about both throughput — we process spikes of a few thousand concurrent chats — and tight tail latency because agents expect sub-200 millisecond suggestions.
[00:01:04] Ethan: Nice, and where were you before Redwood?
[00:01:08] Rahul: We tried a mix. Initially hosted endpoints from a few providers, higher-tier managed APIs when we needed quality, but costs ballooned and tail latency was inconsistent. We also prototyped self-hosting open models but the ops burden was high.
[00:01:26] [00:01:30] Priya N.: Can you describe the tipping point when you decided to run a pilot with Redwood?
[00:01:34] Liam: The tipping point was predictable economics — we saw that at our scale even small per-token differences mattered. Plus we wanted an ops-lite path that still gave us control: hints of private deployment, but without having to own low-level GPU infra right away.
[00:01:54] [00:02:00] Ethan: And the pilot — what did it look like? Dedicated pool? A/B?
[00:02:05] Priya S.: We started with a Dedicated pool on Redwood. We ran a 3-week pilot with a shadow A/B against our incumbent provider for a subset of traffic, measured latency, cost per 1k tokens, and regression in suggestion quality on our eval prompts.
[00:02:23] [00:02:26] Liam: I'll add that the Redwood team helped us set up KV caching and batching rules; that shaved a ton off token costs. Though the transcript might say 'KV cash' later — ha.
[00:02:36] Priya N.: (laughs) transcribers.
[00:02:40] [00:02:45] Ethan: Any specific numbers you can share from the pilot? Even ballpark is great for listeners.
[00:02:49] Rahul: Sure, roughly — p95 latency for the common short prompts dropped from about 320ms to ~120ms. Token cost per 1k fell by about 40% after applying batching and the auto-cache hints. Our overall throughput margin grew enough to avoid a planned 30% cluster expansion.
[00:03:09] [00:03:15] Priya S.: On quality we had a sub-2% regression on our critical evals, which we deemed acceptable given the latency/cost improvements. We iterated on prompting and warmed some of the prefix caches to recover quality.
[00:03:29] [00:03:35] Maya: That's fantastic. For the story, can you talk about who's involved internally — which stakeholders made the decision and what the procurement timeline looked like?
[00:03:43] Liam: Tech-led decision: Rahul and I championed it, engineering budget approved it. Procurement and legal ran a quick security review — Redwood's SOC 2 docs and KMS/HSM integration were important. We went from pilot to committed Dedicated capacity in about six weeks.
[00:04:03] [00:04:10] Ethan: Speaking of security, were there any specific compliance or data residency asks you had?
[00:04:14] Priya S.: Our enterprise customers demanded that logs be controllable and that PII was handled according to our policies. Redwood's retain/erase hooks and audit logs were crucial. We also asked about VPC/private deployment for a subset of sensitive tenants — that's on the roadmap now.
[00:04:31] [00:04:36] Priya N.: We flagged that you might want Private eventually; good to hear it's on your roadmap.
[00:04:40] [00:04:45] Liam: Yeah, it's a future phase. For now Dedicated hits our needs and gives us the SLA predictability.
[00:04:51] [00:04:58] Ethan: For listeners who love nerdy details, can you explain one thing the Redwood SEs helped optimize that surprised you?
[00:05:04] Rahul: Two things — the way batching and sequence length distribution interplay. We had a lot of short prompts; Redwood suggested batching windows tuned to our 95th percentiles which improved GPU utilization. Also the prefix caching — by caching stabilized conversation prefixes we avoided recomputing early attention layers and that dropped compute on repeated patterns. The SEs even provided a small script that simulated our traffic to recommend batching sizes.
[00:05:33] [00:05:40] Priya N.: We also surfaced quantization recommendations — a mixed precision profile that kept quality within thresholds while saving memory; that allowed larger batch sizes.
[00:05:49] [00:05:55] Liam: The combination of those levers is what made the cost delta real.
[00:05:59] [00:06:05] Maya: There's often a fear that these platform optimizations add complexity to the product team — did you find that to be true?
[00:06:10] Priya S.: It added some initial tuning work but Redwood's default policies were good. SE-led runbooks helped standardize it so our SREs could operationalize without constant SE help.
[00:06:21] [00:06:28] Ethan: Great. For the marketing piece, we'd love a quote about business impact — Rahul, you mentioned avoiding a cluster expansion; anything you want to frame as a one-liner?
[00:06:36] Rahul: Sure: "Switching to Redwood reduced our per-query cost and improved latency enough that we delayed a major infra expansion, saving months of ops work and capex."
[00:06:48] [00:06:55] Maya: Perfect — we'll polish that and send it for approval.
[00:06:59] [00:07:03] Priya N.: Quick tangent — competitors were mentioned during the evaluation. Any notes on why you picked Redwood over others?
[00:07:08] Liam: Two things: 1) predictable economics and a clear path from hosted to dedicated/private, and 2) the SE engagement — they ran realistic benchmarks and didn't overpromise. OpenAI/Anthropic had great base models but the cost delta and the ability to control hosting choices made Redwood compelling.
[00:07:30] [00:07:36] Ethan: Makes sense. Anything that surprised you or was harder than expected?
[00:07:41] Priya S.: We underestimated the first-week tuning for caching behavior — it required careful prompt normalization. Also logs and telemetry needed mapping into our existing observability to get the full picture.
[00:07:56] [00:08:02] Liam: And handling spike tail behavior — classic cloud patterns — we worked with Redwood to set burst policies to keep SLAs intact during peak support hours.
[00:08:12] [00:08:20] Maya: For the podcast listeners, do you have a piece of advice for teams considering a similar path?
[00:08:25] Rahul: Build good eval sets first. If you can't quantify acceptable regression, it's easy to get lost in noise. Also, run a shadow A/B with real traffic — synthetic tests don't reveal tail latency quirks.
[00:08:42] [00:08:47] Priya S.: And don't ignore prompt engineering — small prompt rewrites plus caching can yield outsized wins.
[00:08:53] [00:08:58] Ethan: Nice. Switching to logistics — Maya will draft the case study. We're hoping to include a short 2-minute recorded quote from Rahul and a 30-second product-focused snippet from Liam. Is everyone ok with that?
[00:09:09] Liam: Yes.
[00:09:11] Rahul: Yep, fine by me.
[00:09:14] [00:09:20] Maya: We'll also anonymize any customer-identifiable metrics if required — Priya S., you'll approve wording?
[00:09:25] Priya S.: Yup, as long as it's aggregated or anonymized.
[00:09:29] [00:09:35] Ethan: Any other customer anecdotes you want in the story — maybe an engineering anti-pattern you fixed?
[00:09:40] Liam: One small anecdote — before Redwood we used long context windows for a single pass which was expensive; we refactored to keep short high-signal context plus a summary state. That reduced working set and made caching effective.
[00:09:55] [00:10:00] Priya N.: Love that — product insight and ops win.
[00:10:03] [00:10:10] Ethan: Quick audience question — what metrics will you let us publish? Total queries per day? cost percent improvement?
[00:10:17] Rahul: Publish percent improvement in token cost and p95 latency improvements in relative terms, not absolute revenue numbers. We'll approve exact wording.
[00:10:27] [00:10:35] Maya: Great. We'll draft and send.

[00:12:05] Ethan: Okay, wrapping toward anecdotal stuff — Liam, what's one user-facing thing that improved since you switched?
[00:12:12] Liam: Faster agent suggestions — agents told us the suggested reply was noticeably snappier, reduced cognitive load and time-to-resolve on some cases. We saw small but measurable improvements in agent NPS in a limited rollout.
[00:12:28] [00:12:35] Priya S.: We also stopped seeing timeouts during peak; that was literally a UX win.
[00:12:40] [00:12:45] Ethan: Nice. Any words about costs — is it now a predictable monthly budget line?
[00:12:51] Rahul: Much more predictable. Dedicated committed capacity smoothed out spikes and the unit economics are stable once you tune batching and caching.
[00:12:59] [00:13:05] Priya N.: A note for listeners — many teams conflate average latency with p95. Make sure you instrument p95 for interactive workloads.
[00:13:13] [00:13:20] Maya: Final marketing question — anything off-limits for the case study?
[00:13:24] Priya S.: Don't disclose any customer PII, don't disclose per-customer revenues or contract terms. Otherwise technical details and aggregate metrics are fine.

[00:13:58] Priya N.: Thanks! Happy to help.
